\begin{array}{c} - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \lambda \frac {1}{T} [ \nabla T ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu   d s _ {x} - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} [ \varrho s ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} V   d s _ {x} \\ = \int_ {\Omega} \lambda   T ^ {2} | \nabla (\frac {1}{T}) | ^ {2}   d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \varrho \big [ \frac {u}{T} - s \big ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} V   d s _ {x} \\ = \int_ {\Omega} \lambda   T ^ {2} | \nabla (\frac {1}{T}) | ^ {2}   d x \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

Here, one has to use the free boundary condition (7.52) and the last identity follows from the fact that at the free boundary the free energy $f = u - T s$ is continuous, i.e., 

$$
\left[ \frac {u}{T} - s \right] _ {s} ^ {\ell} = \left[ \frac {f}{T} \right] _ {s} ^ {\ell} = \frac {c _ {V} T _ {M} + L}{T _ {M}} - \frac {L}{T _ {M}} - \frac {c _ {V} T _ {M}}{T _ {M}} = 0.
$$

Altogether, we showed that the total entropy cannot decrease. This condition is necessary in order to fulfill the second law of thermodynamics. In fact, another inequality is true which has important consequences for the analysis of the Stefan problem. With the transport theorem we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} d x = \int_ {\Omega_ {\ell} (t)} \varrho c _ {V} (T - T _ {M}) \partial_ {t} T d x \\ \qquad + \int_ {\Omega_ {s} (t)} \varrho c _ {V} (T - T _ {M}) \partial_ {t} T d x - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \left[ \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} \right] _ {s} ^ {\ell} V d s _ {x} \\ = \int_ {\Omega_ {\ell} (t)} \lambda (T - T _ {M}) \Delta T d x + \int_ {\Omega_ {s} (t)} \lambda (T - T _ {M}) \Delta T d x \\ = - \int_ {\Omega_ {\ell} (t)} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2} d x - \int_ {\Omega_ {s} (t)} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2} d x - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \lambda [ \nabla T ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu (T - T _ {M}) d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

The integrals with respect to $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ vanish due to the fact that $T = T _ { M }$ on $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ Altogether we obtain 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Omega} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2} d x = 0.
$$

This equality is the basis for an existence proof using techniques of functional analysis. 

## 7.5 Undercooled Liquids

So far we assumed that the liquid phase is characterized by $T > T _ { M }$ and that the solid phase is characterized by $T < T _ { M }$ . In fact, it is possible that liquids are undercooled and that solids are superheated. It may happen, for instance, that liquids remain in the liquid phase even when the temperature in the liquid is below the melting temperature. 

We now want to study this situation for an idealized model system. Now we set $u = T - T _ { M }$ . Notice that u here and in the Sects. 7.5–7.7 will not denote the density of the internal energy. We consider the growth of a crystal nucleus which at time $t = 0$ only consists of one point. In addition, we assume the following: 

Spatially the temperature only varies in one direction and we have $u = u ( t , x )$ with $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

The phase boundary is orthogonal to the x-axis. 

The location of the phase boundary is denoted by $y ( t ) \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ and it holds $y ( 0 ) =$ 0. We assume that points $x < y ( t )$ are in the solid phase and points with $x > y ( t )$ are in the liquid phase. 

The diffusion constant is large, or more precisely, $\frac { \varrho c _ { V } } { \lambda }$ is small. In this case we can consider the quasi-stationary equation 

$$
u _ {x x} (t, x) = 0, x \in (0, 1), x \neq y (t), t > 0
$$

instead of the heat equation. 

The left boundary is isolated and at the right boundary we prescribe the constant temperature U, i.e., for a $U \in \mathbb { R }$ we require 

$$
u _ {x} (t, 0) = 0, u (t, 1) = U, t > 0.
$$

Denoting by $u ( t , x - )$ and $u ( t , x + )$ the limit with respect to x from the left and the right, respectively, we obtain the following problem: 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u _ {x x} (t, x) = 0 \text {for} x \in (0, 1), x \neq y (t), t > 0, \\ u (t, y (t)) = 0 \text {for} t > 0, \\ \varrho L V = \varrho L y ^ {\prime} (t) = \lambda (u _ {x} (t, y (t) -) - u _ {x} (t, y (t) +)) \text {for} t > 0, \\ y (0) = 0, \\ u _ {x} (t, 0) = 0, u (t, 1) = U. \end{array}
$$

The solution is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u (t, x) = 0 \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq y (t), \\ u (t, x) = U \frac {x - y (t)}{1 - y (t)} \text { for } y (t) <   x \leq 1. \end{array}
$$

In addition, it holds 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varrho L y ^ {\prime} (t) = - \lambda \frac {U}{1 - y (t)}, \\ y (0) = 0. \end{array}
$$

Hence, for $U = 0$ we have no movement of the phase boundary. For $U > 0$ we obtain $y ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) \leq 0$ and the phase boundary cannot move into the liquid region. On the other hand if $U < 0$ we obtain 

$$
y (t) = 1 - \left(1 + 2 \frac {\lambda}{\varrho L} U t\right) ^ {1 / 2}.
$$

We hence observe that the crystal nucleus can only grow if the liquid is undercooled. 

For solidification the form of the phase boundary plays an important role. If the phase boundary is curved then the temperature at the phase boundary will deviate from the melting temperature $T _ { M }$ due to capillary effects. For a round solid nucleus the temperature at which solidification happens is below the melting temperature. The temperature will in fact depend on the curvature of the phase boundary (Gibbs– Thomson effect). We will see later that the Gibbs–Thomson effect has a stabilizing effect on solidification. In order to formulate the Gibbs–Thomson condition at the phase boundary we need the notion of mean curvature which is introduced in Appendix B. 

## 7.6 Gibbs–Thomson Effect

We will now consider undercooling and superheating and in addition take into account that the melting temperature at the phase boundary can depend on the curvature. More precisely, we consider the Mullins–Sekerka problem for the scaled temperature $\begin{array} { r } { u = \frac { \bar { \lambda } } { \varrho L } ( T - \bar { T } _ { M } ) } \end{array}$ 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \Delta u = 0 & \text { in } \Omega_ {s} (t) \cup \Omega_ {\ell} (t)  , \\ V = - [ \nabla u ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu \text { on } \Gamma (t)  , \\ u = \gamma \kappa & \text { on } \Gamma (t)  . \end{array} \right.\tag{7.57}
$$

Here $\gamma$ is a suitable scaled surface tension and κ is the sum of the principle curvatures which we will call the mean curvature in what follows, cf. Appendix B. The sign of $\kappa$ is chosen such that $\kappa < 0$ for a strictly convex solid. The Laplace equation is obtained as a quasi-static variant of the Stefan problem which we derived in the previous sections. This means we assume that $\frac { \varrho c _ { V } } { \lambda }$ is small, which implies that the time derivative in the heat equation can be neglected. The last equation in (7.57) is the Gibbs–Thomson condition and this condition allows for an undercooling due to the curvature. This means for example that the temperature at the phase boundary for a convex nucleus can be below the melting temperature. 

We will now analyze under which conditions a crystal nucleus can grow. In order to do so we now consider the Mullins–Sekerka problem (7.57) with 

$$
\Omega = B _ {R} (0) \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {3}, \Omega_ {s} (0) = B _ {r _ {0}} (0), \Gamma (0) = \partial B _ {r _ {0}} (0), \Omega_ {\ell} (0) = B _ {R} (0) \setminus \overline {{B _ {r _ {0}} (0)}},
$$

where $0 < r _ { 0 } < R < \infty$ . On the exterior boundary we prescribe a fixed temperature underneath the melting temperature: 

$$
u (t, x) = u _ {0} \equiv \text { const } <   0 \quad \text { for } \quad x \in \partial \Omega , t > 0.\tag{7.58}
$$

We are looking for a radial solution $u ( t , x ) = v ( t , | x | )$ with $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t ) = \partial B _ { r ( t ) } ( 0 )$ . As $\begin{array} { r } { \kappa ( t ) = - \frac { 2 } { r ( t ) } } \end{array}$ on $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ we obtain in the solid phase 

$$
v (t, r) = - \frac {2 \gamma}{r (t)} \text { for   all } r \in [ 0, r (t) ].
$$

For $d = 3$ we obtain $\begin{array} { r } { \varDelta _ { x } v ( | x | ) = v ^ { \prime \prime } ( | x | ) + \frac { 2 } { | x | } v ^ { \prime } ( | x | ) } \end{array}$ , cf. (6.12). From (7.57) we deduce 

$$
0 = v ^ {\prime \prime} + \frac {2}{r} v ^ {\prime} \text { or } 0 = (r ^ {2} v ^ {\prime}) ^ {\prime}.
$$

We hence obtain 

$$
v (t, r) = c _ {1} (t) \frac {1}{r} + c _ {2} (t), c _ {1} (t), c _ {2} (t) \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

The Gibbs–Thomson condition and the boundary condition (7.58) yield the following boundary conditions in the liquid phase 

$$
c _ {1} (t) \frac {1}{R} + c _ {2} (t) = u _ {0} \text { and } c _ {1} (t) \frac {1}{r (t)} + c _ {2} (t) = - \frac {2 \gamma}{r (t)}.
$$

From this we compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} c _ {1} (t) = \left(u _ {0} + \frac {2 \gamma}{r (t)}\right) / \left(\frac {1}{R} - \frac {1}{r (t)}\right) = (\gamma   \kappa (t) - u _ {0}) / \left(\frac {1}{r (t)} - \frac {1}{R}\right), \\ c _ {2} (t) = - \frac {1}{r (t)} (2 \gamma + c _ {1}). \end{array}
$$

As $V = { \dot { r } } ( t )$ the Stefan condition in (7.57) implies 

$$
\dot {r} (t) = c _ {1} (t) \frac {1}{r (t) ^ {2}} = (\gamma \kappa (t) - u _ {0}) / \left(\frac {1}{r (t) ^ {3}} - \frac {1}{r (t) ^ {2} R}\right).\tag{7.59}
$$

The right-hand side is zero if and only if 

$$
\gamma \kappa = u _ {0} \text {   and   hence   } r = - \frac {2 \gamma}{u _ {0}}.
$$

The radius $\begin{array} { r } { r _ { \mathrm { c r i t } } = - \frac { 2 \gamma } { u _ { 0 } } } \end{array}$ is called critical radius. For $r _ { 0 } < r _ { \mathrm { c r i t } }$ The right-hand side in (7.59) is negative at initial time and a nucleus which is too small will vanish in finite time. For $r _ { 0 } > r _ { \mathrm { c r i t } }$ we obtain that the nucleus will grow. In addition, it holds 

for large undercooling $r _ { \mathrm { c r i t } }$ is small, 

for small undercooling $r _ { \mathrm { c r i t } }$ is large. 

A nucleus has to have a certain size to be able to grow. For large undercooling also small nuclei can grow. 

## 7.7 Mullins–Sekerka Instability

In the previous section we saw that a nucleus can only grow if the surrounding is undercooled. The analysis in this section will show that a phase boundary which grows into an undercooled fluid is unstable. 

We consider a solidification process in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ where the coordinates are denoted by $( x , y ) ^ { \top }$ . We consider a solidification front which is parallel to the x-axis and which grows with velocity $V _ { 0 }$ in the direction of the y-axis. For $y  + \infty$ and $y  - \infty$ we prescribe the heat fluxes 

$$
- \nabla u = - g _ {\ell} \binom{0}{1} \quad \text { and } \quad - \nabla u = - g _ {s} \binom{0}{1}.
$$

We consider a coordinate system which moves with the solidification front, such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Omega_ {\ell} (t) = \{(x, y) ^ {\top} | y > 0 \}, \\ \Omega_ {s} (t) = \{(x, y) ^ {\top} | y <   0 \}. \end{array}
$$

In this geometry we consider the following solution of the Mullins–Sekerka problem (7.57) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {s} (x, y) = g _ {s}   y \text {   for   } y <   0  , \\ u _ {\ell} (x, y) = g _ {\ell}   y \text {   for   } y > 0  . \end{array}
$$

With $\nabla u _ { s } = ( 0 , g _ { s } ) ^ { \top }$ for $y < 0 , \nabla u _ { \ell } = ( 0 , g _ { \ell } ) ^ { \top }$ for $y > 0$ and $ { \boldsymbol \nu } = ( 0 , 1 ) ^ { \top }$ we obtain 

$$
[ \nabla u ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu = g _ {\ell} - g _ {s},
$$

and hence 

$$
V _ {0} = g _ {s} - g _ {\ell}.
$$

In addition, the condition $u = 0$ holds on the phase boundary $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } = \{ ( x , y ) \mid y = 0 \}$ 

We now analyze whether the phase boundary is stable with respect to small perturbations. We now perturb the flat phase boundary at initial time with a sinusoidal profile with a small amplitude $\delta ( 0 )$ and a period $\frac { 2 \pi } { \omega }$ . In the moving coordinate system such a perturbed phase boundary is given by 

$$
y = h (t, x) = \delta (t) \sin (\omega x) \text { with } \omega > 0.
$$

Since we perturbed the phase boundary with a certain wavelength we also make an ansatz for the solution with the same wavelength. This ansatz would also be obtained from an ansatz with separation of variables. Hence we make the ansatz 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {s} (t, x, y) = g _ {s}   y + c _ {s} (t)   e ^ {\omega y} \sin (\omega x), \\ u _ {\ell} (t, x, y) = g _ {\ell}   y + c _ {\ell} (t)   e ^ {- \omega y} \sin (\omega x). \end{array}
$$

These functions solve the Laplace equation $\varDelta u = 0$ and we ensure that for large $| y |$ the perturbation decays. Far away from the phase boundary we prescribe the temperature gradient and hence we prescribe the heat flux. 

We want to guarantee that $u _ { \ell }$ and $u _ { s }$ fulfill the conditions at the free boundary at least approximately. In order to solve the equation $u = \gamma \kappa$ on $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } }$ approximately we compute $u _ { s }$ and $u _ { \ell }$ on the phase boundary as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u _ {s} (t, x, h (t, x)) = g _ {s}   h (t, x) + c _ {s} (t)   e ^ {\omega h (t, x)} \sin (\omega x) \\ \qquad = g _ {s}   \delta (t) \sin (\omega x) + c _ {s} (t)   e ^ {\omega h (t, x)} \sin (\omega x)  , \\ u _ {\ell} (t, x, h (t, x)) = g _ {\ell}   h (t, x) + c _ {\ell} (t)   e ^ {- \omega h (t, x)} \sin (\omega x) \\ \qquad = g _ {\ell}   \delta (t) \sin (\omega x) + c _ {\ell} (t)   e ^ {- \omega h (t, x)} \sin (\omega x)  . \end{array}
$$

Denoting by $\kappa ( t , x )$ the curvature at $( x , h ( t , x ) )$ we obtain (cf. Appendix B) 

$$
\kappa (t, x) = \frac {\partial_ {x x} h}{(1 + (\partial_ {x} h) ^ {2}) ^ {3 / 2}} = \partial_ {x x} h + \mathcal {O} (\delta^ {2}) \approx - \delta (t) \omega^ {2} \sin (\omega x).
$$

In order to fulfill $u = \gamma \kappa \mathrm { u p }$ to an error of the order $\delta ^ { 2 }$ , we require 

$$
c _ {s} (t) = - (\gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {s}) \delta (t),\tag{7.60}
$$

$$
c _ {\ell} (t) = - (\gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {\ell}) \delta (t).\tag{7.61}
$$

We now evaluate the jump condition $V = - [ \nabla u ] _ { s } ^ { \ell } \cdot \boldsymbol \nu$ . With the normal vector 

$$
\nu = \left(1 / \left(1 + (\partial_ {x} h) ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2}\right) (- \partial_ {x} h, 1) ^ {\top}
$$

it follows that 

$$
\nabla u _ {s} = \left(\omega c _ {s} (t) e ^ {\omega y} \cos (\omega x), g _ {s} + \omega c _ {s} (t) e ^ {\omega y} \sin (\omega x)\right) ^ {\top}
$$

and then with (7.60), 

$$
\nabla u _ {s} \cdot \nu_ {| y = h} = g _ {s} - \delta (t) (\gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {s}) \omega \sin (\omega x) + \mathcal {O} (\delta^ {2}).
$$

Analogously we compute with (7.61) 

$$
\nabla u _ {\ell} \cdot \nu_ {| y = h} = g _ {\ell} + \delta (t) (\gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {\ell}) \omega \sin (\omega x) + \mathcal {O} (\delta^ {2}).
$$

It follows that 

$$
- [ \nabla u ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu = g _ {s} - g _ {\ell} - \delta (2 \gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {s} + g _ {\ell}) \omega \sin (\omega x).\tag{7.62}
$$

Besides we obtain as in Sect. 7.3 for the normal velocity $V ( t , x )$ in the point $( x , h ( t , x ) )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} V (t, x) = \binom {0} {V _ {0} + \partial_ {t} h} \cdot \binom {- \partial_ {x} h} {1} \frac {1}{(1 + (\partial_ {x} h) ^ {2}) ^ {1 / 2}} \\ = \frac {V _ {0} + \partial_ {t} h}{(1 + (\partial_ {x} h) ^ {2}) ^ {1 / 2}} = V _ {0} + \delta^ {\prime} (t) \sin (\omega x) + \mathcal {O} (\delta^ {2}). \end{array}
$$

Together with (7.62) we obtain 

$$
\delta^ {\prime} (t) = - \lambda (\omega) \delta (t)
$$

with 

$$
\lambda (\omega) = \omega \{2 \gamma \omega^ {2} + g _ {s} + g _ {\ell} \}.
$$

Hence the perturbations will grow exponentially in time if $\lambda ( \omega ) < 0$ and will be damped if $\lambda ( \omega ) > 0$ . Now let $g _ { s } \geq 0 ,$ , i.e., the temperature in the solid phase is negative. If $g _ { \ell } \geq 0$ then the fluid is not undercooled and we obtain $\lambda ( \omega ) > 0$ and hence this is a stable situation. 

In the case $g _ { \ell } < 0$ the liquid phase is supercooled. There are two cases: 

(i) The case $\gamma = 0$ without capillary term. In case of undercooling 

$$
g _ {\ell} + g _ {s} <   0
$$

all wavelengths are amplified and we obtain a strongly unstable situation. For 

$$
g _ {\ell} + g _ {s} > 0,
$$

we obtain a stable situation. 

(ii) The case $\gamma > 0$ . In this case all small wavelengths, which are perturbations with a large $\omega ,$ are damped. In case of strong undercooling, i.e., in a case where $g _ { \ell }$ is strongly negative, certain large wavelength are unstable. The most unstable wavelengths are obtained for $\omega$ near the positive local minimum $\omega _ { s i }$ of $\lambda .$ . We obtain 

$$
\omega_ {s i} = \sqrt {\frac {- (g _ {s} + g _ {\ell})}{6 \gamma}}
$$

and with our experience from Sects. 6.2.12 and 6.2.13 we expect that the length scale defined by $\omega _ { s i } ^ { - 1 }$ plays an important role in real solidification scenarios with planar fronts. 

Summarizing we observe in the case without capillary term γκ and strong undercooling lead to a very unstable phase boundary. As the formation of new surface costs energy one obtains that the capillary term has a stabilizing effect such that small wavelengths are damped. 

The fact that strongly undercooled fluids have very unstable phase boundaries yield very bifurcated phase boundaries. Many solidification fronts lead to dendritic (tree-like) structures. Variants of the Mullins–Sekerka stability analysis from above are used to explain the diverse patterns observed in snow crystal growth (see, e.g., Libbrecht [88], Barrett et al. [11]). 

## 7.8 A Priori Estimates for the Stefan Problem with Gibbs–Thomson Condition

We introduced the Gibbs–Thomson condition in order to allow for a curvature undercooling. In addition, one often considers a kinetic undercooling which takes into account that the system needs time to evolve into the local equilibrium conditions $T = T _ { M } \mathrm { o r } T - T _ { M } = \gamma \kappa$ . Hence, we now consider the relaxation dynamics 

$$
\beta V = \gamma \kappa - \varrho L (T - T _ {M}) \mathrm{with} \beta \geq 0.\tag{7.63}
$$

Here $\gamma$ is a suitable scaled surface energy density. We note that the scaling here is different to the scaling in Sect. 7.6. The parameter $\beta$ reflects the strength of the kinetic undercooling. We can easily show that the energy conservation law (7.43) also holds with the condition (7.63). We now want to understand the regularizing effect of the terms $\beta V$ and $\gamma \kappa$ a little better. In order to do so, we show that the law (7.63) allows for an estimate of the surface area of the phase boundary. This implies that the phase boundary cannot become arbitrarily irregular. It is a general observation in nature that capillarity has a smoothing effect. To proceed we need the following result. 

Theorem 7.4 For a smooth, compact evolving hypersurface without boundary it holds 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} 1 d s _ {x} = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \kappa V d s _ {x}.
$$

Proof We first give a proof in the similar case that the phase boundary is given by a closed curve in the plane. In this case the proof can be done quite elementary. We consider a smooth function 

$$
y: [ t _ {1}, t _ {2} ] \times [ a, b ] \to \mathbb {R} ^ {2}, (t, p) \mapsto y (t, p)
$$

with $t _ { 1 } < t _ { 2 }$ and $a < b$ such that $y ( t , \cdot )$ is a regular parametrization of $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ . In this case the length element is given by $| \partial _ { p } y |$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { | \partial _ { p } y | } \partial _ { p } \left( \frac { \partial _ { p } y } { | \partial _ { p } y | } \right) = \kappa \nu } \end{array}$ , cf. Appendix B. We can now compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} 1 d s _ {x} = \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {a} ^ {b} | \partial_ {p} y (t, p) | d p = \int_ {a} ^ {b} \left(\frac {\partial_ {p} y}{| \partial_ {p} y |} \cdot \partial_ {t} \partial_ {p} y\right) (t, p) d p \\ = - \int_ {a} ^ {b} \left(\partial_ {p} \frac {\partial_ {p} y}{| \partial_ {p} y |} \cdot \partial_ {t} y\right) (t, p) d p = - \int_ {a} ^ {b} \left(\kappa \nu \cdot \partial_ {t} y   | \partial_ {p} y |\right) (t, p) d p \\ = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \kappa V d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

In the general case we choose a partition of unity $\{ \zeta _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { M }$ of the $\mathbb { R } ^ { 1 + d }$ , such that the surface patches $\Gamma \cap$ supp $\zeta _ { i }$ can be written as a graph as in the proof of Theorem 7.3. We then obtain 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} 1 d s _ {x} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \zeta_ {i} (t, x) d s _ {x}.
$$

As supp $\zeta _ { i } \cap { \cal { T } }$ can be written as a graph of 

$$
h: (t _ {1}, t _ {2}) \times D \to \mathbb {R}, t _ {1} <   t _ {2}, D \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {d - 1} \text { open },
$$

we can compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \zeta_ {i} (t, x) d s _ {x} = \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {D} \zeta_ {i} (t, x ^ {\prime}, h (t, x ^ {\prime})) \sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h (t , x ^ {\prime}) | ^ {2}} d x ^ {\prime} \\ \qquad = \int_ {D} (\partial_ {t} \zeta_ {i} + \partial_ {x _ {d}} \zeta_ {i} \partial_ {t} h) \sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}} d x ^ {\prime} \\ \qquad + \int_ {D} \frac {\zeta_ {i}}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h \cdot \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \partial_ {t} h d x ^ {\prime} \\ \qquad = \int_ {D} (\partial_ {t} \zeta_ {i} + \partial_ {x _ {d}} \zeta_ {i} \partial_ {t} h) \sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}} d x ^ {\prime} \\ \qquad - \int_ {D} \partial_ {t} h \zeta_ {i} \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}}\right) d x ^ {\prime} \\ \qquad - \int_ {D} \left(\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \zeta_ {i} + \partial_ {x _ {d}} \zeta_ {i} \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h\right) \cdot \frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \partial_ {t} h d x ^ {\prime}. \end{array}
$$

Using $\begin{array} { r } { \nu = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 1 + | \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h | ^ { 2 } } } ( - \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h , 1 ) ^ { \top } , \kappa = \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } \cdot \left( \frac { \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h } { \sqrt { 1 + | \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h | ^ { 2 } } } \right) \mathrm { a n d } V = \frac { \partial _ { t } h } { \sqrt { 1 + | \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h | ^ { 2 } } } \mathrm { w e } } \end{array}$ obtain 

7.8 A Priori Estimates for the Stefan Problem with Gibbs–Thomson Condition 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \zeta_ {i} (t, x) d s _ {x} = \int_ {\Gamma (t)} (\nabla \zeta_ {i} \cdot \nu V + \partial_ {t} \zeta_ {i} - \zeta_ {i} V \kappa) d s _ {x}.
$$

By summation with respect to i we obtain the claim by using $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \zeta _ { i } = 1 } \end{array}$ 

To obtain an estimate for the Stefan problem (7.51), (7.52), with Gibbs–Thomson condition and kinetic undercooling (7.63) we first of all compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x} = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma \kappa V d s _ {x} \\ = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \beta V ^ {2} d s _ {x} - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \varrho L V (T - T _ {M}) d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

Here and in the following we always assume that the phase boundary does not intersect the outer boundary Γ. As in Sect. 7.4 one can deduce, using that $T$ is continuous across $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} d x = - \int_ {\Omega} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2} d x - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} (T - T _ {M}) \lambda [ \nabla T ] _ {s} ^ {\ell} \cdot \nu d s _ {x}.
$$

Combining the last two identities we obtain with (7.52) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \left(\int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x}\right) \\ = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \beta V ^ {2} d s _ {x} - \int_ {\Omega} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2} d x. \end{array}\tag{7.64}
$$

The capillary term in the Gibbs–Thomson equation hence yields the surface area of the phase boundary as additional term in the a priori estimate. As additional dissipative term we obtain besides the Dirichlet integral of the temperature the squared $L _ { 2 } \mathrm { - n o r m }$ of the velocity on the boundary. 

We here only considered a simple variant of the Stefan problem with undercooling including capillary and kinetic terms which both lead to a regularization. For a more systematic derivation also of more general models we refer to the book of Gurtin [60]. 

The variant of the Stefan problem with Gibbs–Thomson condition studied so far is the one which is typically used in practice. However, the version studied above is only an approximate theory and in particular does not fulfill the second law of thermodynamics. A simple modification, which then fulfills the second law, is given as follows. The relaxation dynamics (7.63) is replaced by 

$$
\widehat {\beta} V = \widehat {\gamma} \kappa + \varrho L \left(\frac {1}{T} - \frac {1}{T _ {M}}\right)\tag{7.65}
$$

where $\widehat { \beta } , \widehat { \gamma }$ are constants which now have a different physical dimension as the quantities $\beta$ and $\gamma$ in (7.63). It can be shown that (Exercise 7.13) 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \left(\int_ {\Omega} \varrho s d x - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \widehat {\gamma} d s _ {x}\right) \geq 0,\tag{7.66}
$$

where s is the entropy density from Sect. 7.3. The constant $- \widehat { \gamma }$ in this case is an entropy density per area. The above inequality shows that with the modified condition at the free boundary the total entropy can only increase. 

## 7.9 Phase Field Equations

In the Stefan problem the phase boundary is described in the form of a hypersurface. If the free boundary changes its topology, which happens for example in cases where two regions occupied by the solid phase join or in case where a connected region of a solid phase splits into two disconnected regions then this approach has some disadvantages. In all possible descriptions of the hypersurface one will obtain a singularity in the representation of the hypersurface if the topology changes. This is the reason why in the last decades phase-field approaches have been used to describe solidification phenomena. In a phase field model a smooth phase field variable $\varphi$ is introduced which in the solid phase attains values close to 1 and in the liquid phase attains values close to 1. In regions where the phase changes interior layers appear in which the values of $\varphi$ change rapidly. Solutions of the phase field equation remain smooth even in cases where the topological structure of the phase boundary changes. 

The internal energy in the phase field model is given as $u ( T , \varphi ) = c _ { V } T + L { \frac { \varphi + 1 } { 2 } }$ i.e., we interpolate the latent heat in a linear fashion. We then obtain the energy balance 

$$
\partial_ {t} \left(\varrho c _ {V} T + \varrho L \frac {\varphi + 1}{2}\right) = \lambda \Delta T.\tag{7.67}
$$

The $\operatorname { E q } .$ (7.63) for the free boundary is replaced by the equation 

$$
\varepsilon \beta \partial_ {t} \varphi = \varepsilon \gamma \Delta \varphi - \frac {\gamma}{\varepsilon} \psi^ {\prime} (\varphi) + \frac {\varrho L}{2} (T - T _ {M}).\tag{7.68}
$$

Here, $\psi$ is given as $\begin{array} { r } { \psi ( \varphi ) = \frac { 9 } { 3 2 } ( \varphi ^ { 2 } - 1 ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , see Fig. 7.4, and $\varepsilon > 0$ is a parameter which later will turn out to be proportional to the thickness of the interfacial layer. We will see in addition that in an asymptotic expansion for $\varepsilon \to 0$ the term $\partial _ { t } \varphi$ will lead to the negative normal velocity and the term $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon \varDelta \varphi - \frac { 1 } { \varepsilon } \psi ^ { \prime } ( \varphi ) } \end{array}$ will lead to the negative mean curvature. 

Assuming homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions $\nabla T \cdot n = \nabla \varphi \cdot n = 0$ we obtain for smooth solutions of (7.67), (7.68) 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/6ca3d45b-9791-48de-a769-d03e55d18dc9/18dac5ce9ccf6f52ee519f67411ccb658a356d50c54e07c67c6e1523e0c657eb.jpg)



Fig. 7.4 The energy contribution $\psi ( \varphi )$ in (7.70) penalizes values of $\varphi$ which differ strongly from 1


$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \left(\int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} \frac {1}{2} (T - T _ {M}) ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Omega} \gamma \left(\frac {\varepsilon}{2} | \nabla \varphi | ^ {2} + \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \psi (\varphi)\right) d x\right) \\ = \int_ {\Omega} \varrho c _ {V} (T - T _ {M})   \partial_ {t} T   d x + \int_ {\Omega} \gamma \left(\varepsilon \nabla \varphi \cdot \partial_ {t} \nabla \varphi + \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \psi^ {\prime} (\varphi) \partial_ {t} \varphi\right) d x \\ = - \int_ {\Omega} \varrho (T - T _ {M}) \frac {L}{2} \partial_ {t} \varphi   d x + \int_ {\Omega} \lambda \Delta T   (T - T _ {M})   d x \\ + \int_ {\Omega} \gamma \left(- \varepsilon \Delta \varphi + \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \psi^ {\prime} (\varphi)\right) \partial_ {t} \varphi   d x \\ = - \int_ {\Omega} \varepsilon \beta | \partial_ {t} \varphi | ^ {2}   d x - \int_ {\Omega} \lambda | \nabla T | ^ {2}   d x  . \end{array}\tag{7.69}
$$

Comparing this identity with (7.64) we can conjecture that the term 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} \gamma \left(\frac {\varepsilon}{2} | \nabla \varphi | ^ {2} + \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \psi (\varphi)\right) d x\tag{7.70}
$$

corresponds to the capillary term $\int _ { \cal T } \gamma d s _ { x }$ . This can be shown with the help of a suitable limiting process, see [99]. In this context we remark that the gradient term $\scriptstyle { \frac { \varepsilon } { 2 } } \mid \nabla \varphi \mid ^ { 2 }$ in (7.70) penalizes strong spatial changes in the phase field variables. The term $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { \varepsilon } } \psi ( \varphi )$ in (7.70) will become large for small $\varepsilon \operatorname { i f } \varphi$ attains values which differ strongly from 1, compare Fig. 7.4. Solutions $( T , \varphi )$ of the phase field system (7.67), (7.68) hence typically lead to “diffuse” phase boundaries, see Figs. 7.5 and 7.6. 

We now want to show with the help of formal asymptotic analysis that solutions of $( 7 . 6 7 ) { - } ( 7 . 6 8 )$ converge to solutions of the Stefan problem with Gibbs–Thomson condition and kinetic undercooling. We now consider solutions $( T ^ { \varepsilon } , \varphi ^ { \varepsilon } )$ of (7.67), (7.68). For simplicity we consider an $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ and we assume that the sets 

$$
\Gamma^ {\varepsilon} = \{(t, x) \in [ 0, T ] \times \Omega \mid \varphi^ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = 0 \} \text {   for   } \varepsilon > 0
$$

Fig. 7.5 Typical behavior of the phase field variable $\varphi .$ . Regions in which $\varphi \approx \pm 1$ are separated by a “diffuse” phase boundary with a thickness which is proportional to ε


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/6ca3d45b-9791-48de-a769-d03e55d18dc9/60cc8276bbd3a3cb9dd8148b95529e163fcef9e2005b1ff51df6da00d21e6884.jpg)



Fig. 7.6 The phase field variable forms a phase boundary whose thickness is proportional to $\varepsilon$


are evolving hypersurfaces which for all times do not intersect the boundary of $\varOmega$ In addition we assume that the $T ^ { \varepsilon }$ converge towards an evolving hypersurface $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ in a sense which will be made precise later. Now let $y ( t , s )$ be a smooth function which for all t is an arc-length parametrization of $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ^ { 0 } ( t )$ . In addition, let $\nu ( t , s )$ be the unit normal at $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ^ { 0 } ( t )$ in the point $y ( t , s )$ which points into the liquid phase. The parametrization is assumed to be oriented such that $( \nu , \tau )$ with the tangent 

$$
\tau (t, s) = \partial_ {s} y (t, s)
$$

is positively oriented. 

In addition, we assume that we can parametrize $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ^ { \varepsilon } ( t )$ with the help of $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ^ { 0 } ( t )$ as follows 

$$
y ^ {\varepsilon} (t, s) = y (t, s) + d ^ {\varepsilon} (t, s) \nu (t, s).
$$

The hypersurfaces $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ^ { \varepsilon } ( t )$ converge to $\Gamma ^ { 0 } ( t ) \operatorname { i f } d ^ { \varepsilon } \to 0 \operatorname { a s } \varepsilon \to 0$ . We make the ansatz 

$$
d ^ {\varepsilon} (t, s) = d _ {0} (t, s) + \varepsilon d _ {1} (t, s) + \dots .
$$

The convergence of $T ^ { \varepsilon }$ to $T ^ { 0 }$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ means that 

$$
d _ {0} \equiv 0.
$$

In the set $\varOmega \setminus { \cal T } ^ { 0 } ( t )$ we will make an outer expansion and in the neighborhood of $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ we make an ansatz with an inner expansion in a similar way as in Sect. 6.6. For the outer expansion we make the ansatz 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T ^ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = T _ {0} (t, x) + \varepsilon   T _ {1} (t, x) + \dots , \\ \varphi^ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = \varphi_ {0} (t, x) + \varepsilon   \varphi_ {1} (t, x) + \dots . \end{array}
$$

Plugging this ansatz in the Eq. (7.68) we obtain to leading order after a Taylor expansion 

$$
\psi^ {\prime} (\varphi_ {0}) = 0.
$$

This equation has the solutions $\varphi _ { 0 } = - 1 , \varphi _ { 0 } = 0$ and $\varphi _ { 0 } = 1$ . The solutions $\varphi _ { 0 } = 1$ and $\varphi _ { 0 } = - 1$ correspond to the liquid and the solid phase. Since $\psi ^ { \prime \prime } ( 0 ) < 0$ one obtains that $\varphi _ { 0 } = 0$ is an unstable solution of $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon \beta \partial _ { t } \varphi = - \frac { \gamma } { \varepsilon } \psi ^ { \prime } ( \varphi ) } \end{array}$ , and as we expect that unstable solutions are not observed in nature we will not consider this solution any longer. The liquid phase at time t is given by the set 

$$
\Omega_ {\ell} (t) := \{x \in \Omega | \varphi_ {0} (t, x) = 1 \}
$$

and the solid phase at time t is the set 

$$
\Omega_ {s} (t) := \{x \in \Omega \mid \varphi_ {0} (t, x) = - 1 \}.
$$

In both phases the Eq. (7.67) gives to leading order 

$$
\varrho c _ {V} \partial_ {t} T _ {0} = \lambda \Delta T _ {0}.
$$

## Inner Expansion

In the neighborhood ofthe phase boundary $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ we introduce a new coordinate system. We consider the parameter transformation 

$$
F ^ {\varepsilon} (t, s, z) := (t, y (t, s) + \varepsilon z \nu (t, s)).
$$

The variable z describes the ε-scaled signed distance to $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ where we choose a negative sign for points in the solid phase (cf. Exercise 7.14). We now define 

$$
V = \partial_ {t} y \cdot \nu \text { and } V _ {\mathrm{tan}} = \partial_ {t} y \cdot \tau
$$

as the normal velocity and the tangential velocity of the parameterization of the evolving curve $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ and in addition κ is defined to be its curvature. Then (cf. Exercise 7.15) 

$$
\partial_ {s} \tau = \kappa \nu \text { and } \partial_ {s} \nu = - \kappa \tau \text {(Frenet formula)}\tag{7.71}
$$

holds. With this we obtain 

$$
D _ {(t, s, z)} F ^ {\varepsilon} (t, s, z) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \partial_ {t} y + \varepsilon z   \partial_ {t} \nu & (1 - \varepsilon z \kappa) \tau & \varepsilon \nu \end{array} \right).\tag{7.72}
$$

From the identity $\begin{array} { r } { \nu \cdot \partial _ { t } \nu = \frac { 1 } { \gamma } \partial _ { t } | \nu | ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { \gamma } \partial _ { t } 1 = 0 } \end{array}$ we derive with $( t , x ) = F ^ { \varepsilon } ( t , s , z )$ and $( F ^ { \varepsilon } ) ^ { - 1 } ( t , x ) = : ( t , s ( t , \bar { x } ) , z ( t , x ) )$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left( \begin{array}{c c} \partial_ {t} t (t, x) & D _ {x} t (t, x) \\ \partial_ {t} s (t, x) & D _ {x} s (t, x) \\ \partial_ {t} z (t, x) & D _ {x} z (t, x) \end{array} \right) = (D F _ {\varepsilon}) ^ {- 1} (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & (0, 0) \\ - \frac {1}{1 - \varepsilon \kappa z} (V _ {\tan} + \varepsilon z   \tau \cdot \partial_ {t} \nu) & \frac {1}{1 - \varepsilon \kappa z} \tau^ {\top} \\ - \frac {1}{\varepsilon} V & \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \nu^ {\top} \end{array} \right). \end{array}\tag{7.73}
$$

Using the chain rule we obtain for a scalar function $b ( t , s , z )$ and a vector field $j ( t , s , z )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} b (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) = - \frac {1}{\varepsilon} V \partial_ {z} b + \mathcal {O} (1), \\ \nabla_ {x} b (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) = \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \partial_ {z} b \nu + \big (1 + \varepsilon \kappa z + \mathcal {O} \big (\varepsilon^ {2} \big) \big) \partial_ {s} b \tau , \\ \nabla_ {x} \cdot j (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) = \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \partial_ {z} j \cdot \nu + (1 + \varepsilon \kappa z) \partial_ {s} j \cdot \tau + \mathcal {O} \big (\varepsilon^ {2} \big), \\ \Delta_ {x} b (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) = \nabla_ {x} \cdot \big (\nabla_ {x} b (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)) \big) \\ = \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {2}} \partial_ {z z} b - \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \kappa   \partial_ {z} b - \kappa^ {2} z   \partial_ {z} b + \partial_ {s s} b + \mathcal {O} (\varepsilon). \end{array}
$$

In the neighborhood of the phase boundary we introduce the new coordinates and define functions $\Theta ^ { \varepsilon }$ and $\varPhi ^ { \varepsilon }$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T ^ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = \Theta^ {\varepsilon} (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)), \\ \varphi^ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = \Phi^ {\varepsilon} (t, s (t, x), z (t, x)). \end{array}
$$

We expand $\Theta ^ { \varepsilon }$ and $\varPhi ^ { \varepsilon }$ in these new variables 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Theta^ {\varepsilon} (t, s, z) = \Theta_ {0} (t, s, z) + \varepsilon   \Theta_ {1} (t, s, z) + \dots , \\ \Phi^ {\varepsilon} (t, s, z) = \Phi_ {0} (t, s, z) + \varepsilon   \Phi_ {1} (t, s, z) + \dots . \end{array}
$$

The phase field Eq. (7.68) yields to leading order 

$$
0 = \partial_ {z z} \Phi_ {0} - \psi^ {\prime} (\Phi_ {0}).\tag{7.74}
$$

Now and also later we need matching conditions relating inner and outer solutions to obtain boundary conditions for $z  \pm \infty$ . We will now derive these conditions for all orders that we will need later. 

## Matching Conditions

Let us introduce the variable $r = z \varepsilon$ and write the function $\varphi _ { k }$ in the variables $( t , s , r )$ as follows 

$$
\varphi_ {k} (t, x) = \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, r), k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots .
$$

In addition, we assume that the functions $\varphi _ { k }$ from both sides can be smoothly extended onto $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ^ { 0 }$ . Taylor expansion close to $r = 0$ yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, r) = \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, 0 +) + \partial_ {r} \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, 0 +) r + \dots \quad \text { for } r > 0 \text { small }, \\ \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, r) = \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, 0 -) + \partial_ {r} \widehat {\varphi} _ {k} (t, s, 0 -) r + \dots \quad \text { for } r <   0 \text { small }. \end{array}
$$

We expect that the functions $\phi _ { k } ( t , s , z )$ for large z can be approximated by a polynomial in z, i.e., for al $k \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ there exists an $n _ { k } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
\Phi_ {k} (t, s, z) \approx \Phi_ {k, 0} ^ {\pm} (t, s) + \Phi_ {k, 1} ^ {\pm} (t, s) z + \dots + \Phi_ {k, n _ {k}} ^ {\pm} (t, s) z ^ {n _ {k}} \text { for } z \rightarrow \pm \infty .
$$

Here we use the notation $f \approx g \operatorname { f o r } z  \pm \infty \operatorname { i f } f - g$ together with all its derivatives with respect to z converge for $z  \pm \infty$ to zero. To obtain the matching condition we consider as in Sect. 6.6 an “intermediate variable” $\begin{array} { r } { r _ { \eta } = \frac { r } { \varepsilon ^ { \alpha } } = \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \alpha } z } \end{array}$ with $0 < \alpha < 1$ and analyze for fixed $r _ { \eta }$ the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ . To simplify the notation we suppress the dependence on t and s in what follows. On the side of the liquid phase we obtain 

$$
\widehat {\varphi} ^ {\varepsilon} (\varepsilon^ {\alpha} r _ {\eta}) = \widehat {\varphi} _ {0} (0 +) + \varepsilon^ {\alpha} \partial_ {r} \widehat {\varphi} _ {0} (0 +) r _ {\eta} + \mathcal {O} \bigl (\varepsilon^ {2 \alpha} \bigr) + \varepsilon \widehat {\varphi} _ {1} (0 +) + \mathcal {O} \bigl (\varepsilon^ {1 + \alpha} \bigr) + \dots
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \widehat {\varPhi} ^ {\varepsilon} (\varepsilon^ {\alpha - 1} r _ {\eta}) = \varPhi_ {0, 0} ^ {+} + \varepsilon^ {\alpha - 1} \varPhi_ {0, 1} ^ {+} r _ {\eta} + \dots + \varepsilon^ {n _ {0} (\alpha - 1)} \varPhi_ {0, n _ {0}} ^ {+} (r _ {\eta}) ^ {n _ {0}} \\ + \varepsilon   \varPhi_ {1, 0} ^ {+} + \varepsilon^ {\alpha}   \varPhi_ {1, 1} ^ {+} r _ {\eta} + \dots + \varepsilon^ {1 + n _ {1} (\alpha - 1)} \varPhi_ {1, n _ {1}} ^ {+} (r _ {\eta}) ^ {n _ {1}} + \dots . \end{array}
$$

We say that the expansions match if $\widehat { \varphi } ^ { \varepsilon }$ and $\widehat { \Phi } ^ { \varepsilon }$ coincide to all orders in $\varepsilon$ and $r _ { \eta }$ . Comparing the coefficients yields 

$$
\Phi_ {0, 0} ^ {+} = \widehat {\varphi} _ {0} (0 +), \quad \Phi_ {0, i} ^ {+} = 0 \text { for } 1 \leq i \leq n _ {0},
$$

$$
\widehat {\varPhi} _ {1, 0} ^ {+} = \widehat {\varphi} _ {1} (0 +), \quad \varPhi_ {1, 1} ^ {+} = \partial_ {r} \widehat {\varphi} _ {0} (0 +), \quad \varPhi_ {1, i} ^ {+} = 0 \text { for } 2 \leq i \leq n _ {1}.
$$

Corresponding equations hold for the solid phase. 

For $x \in T _ { t }$ we denote by $\varphi _ { 0 } ( x \pm ) , \nabla \varphi _ { 0 } ( x \pm )$ the limits of the quantities $\varphi _ { 0 }$ $\nabla \varphi _ { 0 }$ from the liquid and the solid phase, respectively, where we suppressed the t-dependence. As $\partial _ { r } \widehat { \varphi _ { 0 } } ( 0 \pm ) = ( \nabla \varphi _ { 0 } ( x \pm ) \cdot \nu )$ and since 

$$
\Phi_ {1} (t, s, z) \approx \Phi_ {1, 0} ^ {\pm} (t, s) + \Phi_ {1, 1} ^ {\pm} (t, s) z \text {for} z \to \pm \infty
$$

we obtain the matching conditions 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \Phi_ {0} (z) \approx \varphi_ {0} (x \pm), \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} (z) \approx 0, \\ \Phi_ {1} (z) \approx \varphi_ {1} (x \pm) + (\nabla \varphi_ {0} (x \pm) \cdot \nu) z, \\ \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {1} (z) \approx \nabla \varphi_ {0} (x \pm) \cdot \nu \end{array}
$$

which have to hold for $z  \pm \infty$ . Analogous conditions can be shown for the temperature. 

## Conditions at the Phase Boundary

For $\varPhi _ { 0 }$ we obtain the conditions 

$$
\varPhi_ {0} (t, s, z) \to \pm 1 \text { for } z \to \pm \infty .
$$

Multiplying (7.74) by $\partial _ { z } \phi _ { 0 }$ yields 

$$
0 = \frac {d}{d z} \bigl (\frac {1}{2} (\partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0}) ^ {2} - \psi (\varPhi_ {0}) \bigr).
$$

Using the matching condition it follows that 

$$
\frac {1}{2} (\partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0}) ^ {2} = \psi (\varPhi_ {0})
$$

and as $\varPhi _ { 0 }$ is monotonically increasing we obtain 

$$
\partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0} = \sqrt {2 \psi (\varPhi_ {0})}.
$$

Choosing, as stated above, $\begin{array} { r } { \psi ( \varphi ) = \frac { 9 } { 3 2 } ( \varphi ^ { 2 } - 1 ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ we obtain 

$$
\Phi_ {0} (t, s, z) = \tanh \left(\frac {3}{4} z\right)
$$

as a solution. In principle any translation with respect to $z$ is also a solution. However we will see that the final result will be independent of this translation. Considering (7.67) to leading order yields 

$$
0 = \partial_ {z z} \Theta_ {0}.
$$

The matching conditions yield that $\Theta _ { 0 } ( z )$ has to be bounded for $z  \pm \infty$ . We hence obtain that $\Theta _ { 0 } ( z )$ has to be constant and the matching condition yields 

$$
T _ {0} \text {   is   continuous   across   } \Gamma_ {0}  .
$$

The Eq. (7.68) yields to leading order (1) the condition 

$$
\partial_ {z z} \Phi_ {1} - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\Phi_ {0}) \Phi_ {1} = \left(\kappa - \frac {\beta}{\gamma} V\right) \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} - \frac {\varrho L}{2 \gamma} \left(T _ {0} - T _ {M}\right).\tag{7.75}
$$

The left-hand side is the linearization of the operator on the right-hand side in (7.74). The Eq. (7.74) is translation invariant and this fact implies that the linearization has a nontrivial kernel: If $\varPhi _ { 0 } ( z )$ is a solution of (7.74) then we obtain that $\boldsymbol { \phi } _ { 0 } ( z + y )$ is for all $y \in \mathbb R$ a solution of (7.74). This implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & 0 = \frac {d}{d y} \left[ \partial_ {z z} \varPhi_ {0} (z + y) - \psi^ {\prime} (\varPhi_ {0} (z + y)) \right] \\ & \quad = \partial_ {z z} (\partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0} (z + y)) - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\varPhi_ {0} (z + y)) \partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0} (z + y). \end{array}
$$

Setting $y = 0$ we observe: $\partial _ { z } \phi _ { 0 }$ lies in the kernel of the differential operator $\partial _ { z z } \phi -$ $\psi ^ { \prime \prime } ( \phi _ { 0 } ) \phi$ . We obtain for all solutions $\varPhi _ { 1 }$ of (7.75) with $\phi _ { 1 } ( \pm \infty ) = 0$ with the help of integration by parts that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R}} \left(\partial_ {z z} \varPhi_ {1} - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\varPhi_ {0}) \varPhi_ {1}\right) \partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0} d z = \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \varPhi_ {1} \bigl (\partial_ {z z} (\partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0}) - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\varPhi_ {0}) \partial_ {z} \varPhi_ {0} \bigr) d z = 0
$$

holds. This implies that the right-hand side in (7.75) has to fulfill a solvability condition. This condition reads as 

$$
\left(\kappa - \frac {\beta}{\gamma} V\right) \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} | ^ {2} d z - \frac {\varrho L}{2 \gamma} \big (T _ {0} - T _ {M} \big) \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} d z = 0.
$$

Using 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} | ^ {2}   d z = \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {2 \psi (\Phi_ {0})}   d z \\ = \int_ {- 1} ^ {1} \sqrt {2 \psi (y)}   d y = \int_ {- 1} ^ {1} \frac {3}{4} \big (1 - y ^ {2} \big)   d y = 1  , \end{array}
$$

it follows that 

$$
\gamma \kappa - \beta V - \varrho L (T _ {0} - T _ {M}) = 0.
$$

We now want to derive the Stefan condition at the phase boundary. The energy conservation (7.67) yields to the order $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { O } \left( \frac { 1 } { \varepsilon } \right) } \end{array}$ 

$$
- V \varrho \frac {L}{2} \partial_ {z} \Phi_ {0} = \lambda \partial_ {z z} \Theta_ {1}.
$$

It follows that 

$$
- V \frac {\varrho L}{2} \Phi_ {0} = \lambda \partial_ {z} \Theta_ {1} + \alpha (t, s).
$$

The conditions $\phi _ { 0 } ( z )  \pm 1$ and ∂ Θ (z) T (x ) ν for z yield 

$$
- \varrho L V = [ \lambda \nabla T _ {0} \cdot \nu ] _ {s} ^ {\ell}.
$$

By now we derived all conditions which have to hold for the Stefan problem. 

Analogous to (7.64) for the Stefan problem, the estimate (7.69) does not correspond to the entropy inequality. We now want to derive an entropy inequality. In order to achieve this we need to replace the phase field equation by 

$$
\varepsilon \widehat {\beta} \partial_ {t} \varphi = \varepsilon \widehat {\gamma} \Delta \varphi - \frac {\widehat {\gamma}}{\varepsilon} \psi^ {\prime} (\varphi) - \frac {\varrho L}{2} \left(\frac {1}{T} - \frac {1}{T _ {M}}\right)\tag{7.76}
$$

(cf. Exercise 7.18). The system (7.67), (7.76) has been introduced by Penrose and Fife, see [15, 107]. 

The phase field method has found many applications and we refer to Chen [19], Eck, Garcke and Stinner [31], Garcke, Nestler and Stinner [47], Garcke [45] and [46] for more details. 

## 7.10 Free Surfaces in Fluid Mechanics

In this section we want to study the motion of a fluid with a free surface. To simplify the situation we consider the following geometry: At time t the fluid fills the domain 

$$
\Omega (t) = \left\{(x ^ {\prime}, x _ {3}) = (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, x _ {3}) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {3} \mid x ^ {\prime} \in \Omega^ {\prime}, 0 <   x _ {3} <   h (t, x ^ {\prime}) \right\}\tag{7.77}
$$

where $\varOmega ^ { \prime } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ is a bounded domain and $h : [ 0 , T ] \times \varOmega ^ { \prime }  \mathbb { R }$ is a smooth function which only attains positive values. The fluid hence fills a part of a cylindrical volume with base $\varOmega ^ { \prime }$ . We assume that the Navier–Stokes equations for incompressible fluids 

$$
\varrho (\partial_ {t} v + (v \cdot \nabla) v) = \mu \Delta v - \nabla p + \varrho f,\tag{7.78}
$$

$$
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol {v} = 0\tag{7.79}
$$

are fulfilled in 

$$
Q = \{(t, x) \mid x \in \Omega (t) \}.
$$

We only have to specify the conditions on $\partial \varOmega ( t )$ . On the fixed boundary, i.e., for points $\boldsymbol { x } = ( x ^ { \prime } , x _ { 3 } )$ with $x ^ { \prime } \in \partial \varOmega ^ { \prime }$ or $x _ { 3 } = 0$ we specify the no-slip condition 

$$
v (t, x ^ {\prime}, x _ {3}) = 0 \text { if } x ^ {\prime} \in \partial \Omega^ {\prime} \text { or } x _ {3} = 0.\tag{7.80}
$$

The fluid hence adheres to the container boundary. This condition is not always meaningful and in the literature also slip-conditions are discussed. These conditions allow for a velocity different from zero at the boundary, see Exercise 7.24. 

On the free surface 

$$
\Gamma (t) = \left\{(x ^ {\prime}, x _ {3}) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {3} \mid x ^ {\prime} \in \Omega^ {\prime}, x _ {3} = h (t, x ^ {\prime}) \right\}
$$

we demand a kinetic condition. This condition makes sure that the free boundary moves with the velocity of the fluid. A point on the surface which moves with the velocity of the fluid can be described as $( x ^ { \prime } ( t ) , h ( t , x ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) )$ ). This gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \partial_ {t} x ^ {\prime} (t) = (v _ {1}, v _ {2}) (t, x ^ {\prime} (t), h (t, x ^ {\prime} (t))), \\ \frac {d}{d t} h (t, x ^ {\prime} (t)) = v _ {3} (t, x ^ {\prime} (t), h (t, x ^ {\prime} (t))). \end{array}
$$

We hence obtain the kinetic boundary condition 

$$
v _ {3} = \partial_ {t} h + v _ {1} \partial_ {1} h + v _ {2} \partial_ {2} h \quad \text { on } \quad \Gamma (t)  .\tag{7.81}
$$

The forces which act from the fluid on the surface $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ are given, as discussed in the Sects. 5.5 and 5.6, by $\sigma ( - \nu )$ with the stress tensor 

$$
\sigma = \mu (D v + (D v) ^ {\top}) - p I\tag{7.82}
$$

and the normal vector $\begin{array} { r } { \nu = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 1 + | \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h | ^ { 2 } } } \big ( - \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h , 1 \big ) ^ { \top } } \end{array}$ . On the free surface these forces have to be balanced by capillary forces. The capillary forces try to reduce the total surface area. They act in the direction of the normal ν and they are proportional to the mean curvature. We hence obtain the force balance 

$$
\sigma \nu = \gamma \kappa \nu .\tag{7.83}
$$

The tangential parts of σν hence have to be zero and the normal part is proportional to the mean curvature. We now show that for solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations in Ω with boundary conditions (7.80)–(7.83) an energy inequality holds if for the angle between the free surface and the boundary of the container the angle condition 

$$
\triangleleft (\Gamma (t), \partial \Omega) = 9 0 ^ {\circ}\tag{7.84}
$$

holds. The condition (7.84) can be interpreted as boundary condition for the curvature operator κ. From Appendix B it follows that 

$$
\kappa = \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}}\right).
$$

The condition (7.84) yields 

$$
\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h \cdot n _ {\partial \Omega^ {\prime}} = 0\tag{7.85}
$$

and this can be interpreted as a boundary condition for the operator 

$$
\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}}\right).
$$

In Exercise 7.21 it is discussed how models with more general angle conditions can be treated. 

Theorem 7.5 A smooth solution of (7.78)–(7.84)fulfills in the case $f = 0$ the identity 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \left[ \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v (t, x) | ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x} \right] = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \sigma : D v d x \\ = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\mu}{2} \big (D v + D v ^ {\top} \big): \big (D v + D v ^ {\top} \big) d x \\ \leq 0. \end{array}
$$

Proof We only give a proof for the case that $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( t )$ can be written as a graph for all times t, cf. (7.77). With Theorem 7.3 and the identity $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol { \sigma } = \mu \Delta \boldsymbol { v } - \nabla p$ it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} d x = \int_ {\Omega (t)} \varrho   v \cdot \partial_ {t} v   d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} V   d s _ {x} \\ = \int_ {\Omega (t)} \big (- \varrho   v \cdot (v \cdot \nabla) v + (\nabla \cdot \sigma) \cdot v \big)   d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} V   d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

Here, $\varOmega$ plays the role of $\varOmega _ { s }$ in Theorem 7.3 and $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 } \setminus \varOmega$ takes the role of $\varOmega _ { \ell }$ . In addition, $\frac { \varrho } { 2 } \vert v \vert ^ { 2 }$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 } \setminus \varOmega$ . It holds that $\begin{array} { r } { \boldsymbol { v } \cdot ( \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \nabla ) \boldsymbol { v } = \frac { 1 } { \gamma } \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \nabla | \boldsymbol { v } | ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ and as $v$ is divergence free we obtain after integration by parts and by using the boundary conditions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} d x = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \sigma : D v d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} (V - v \cdot \nu) d s _ {x} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} v \cdot \sigma \nu d s _ {x} \\ \qquad = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \sigma : D v d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} (v \cdot \nu) \gamma \kappa d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

Here we used in the last step that $\begin{array} { r } { \nu = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 1 + | \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h | ^ { 2 } } } ( - \nabla _ { x ^ { \prime } } h , 1 ) } \end{array}$ ) implies 

$$
v \cdot \nu = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} (- v _ {1} \partial_ {1} h - v _ {2} \partial_ {2} h + v _ {3}) = \frac {\partial_ {t} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} = V.
$$

Using the angle condition (7.84) or (7.85) it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x} = \frac {d}{d t} \int_ {\Omega^ {\prime}} \gamma \sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}} d x ^ {\prime} \\ = \int_ {\Omega^ {\prime}} \frac {\gamma}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h \cdot \nabla \partial_ {t} h d x ^ {\prime} = - \int_ {\Omega^ {\prime}} \gamma \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}}\right) \partial_ {t} h d x ^ {\prime} \\ = - \int_ {\Omega^ {\prime}} \gamma \kappa \frac {\partial_ {t} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}} d x ^ {\prime} = - \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma \kappa V d s _ {x}. \end{array}
$$

Altogether we obtain with (7.79), (7.82) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d t} \left[ \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x} \right] = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \sigma : D v d x \\ \qquad = \int_ {\Omega (t)} p \nabla \cdot v d x - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \mu \big (D v + D v ^ {\top} \big): D v d x \\ \qquad = - \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\mu}{2} \big (D v + D v ^ {\top} \big): \big (D v + D v ^ {\top} \big) d x, \end{array}
$$

where in the last identity we used that $D v ^ { \top } : D v ^ { \top } = D v : D v .$ 

Taking into account capillary terms for free surfaces in fluid mechanics hence yields a similar situation as in the Stefan problem with a surface energy term. 

For free surfaces with the Euler equations we set $\mu = 0 \mathrm { i n } ( 7 . 7 8 )$ and the boundary condition (7.83) simplifies to 

$$
p = - \gamma \kappa .\tag{7.86}
$$

In addition, the condition (7.80) changes to 

$$
v (t, x ^ {\prime}, x _ {3}) \cdot n = 0 \text {if} x ^ {\prime} \in \partial \Omega^ {\prime} \text {or} x _ {3} = 0,\tag{7.87}
$$

where n is the exterior unit normal. In this case we obtain for the free surface problem for the Euler equations (see Exercise 7.22) 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \left[ \int_ {\Omega (t)} \frac {\varrho}{2} | v | ^ {2} d x + \int_ {\Gamma (t)} \gamma d s _ {x} \right] = 0.\tag{7.88}
$$

## 7.11 Thin Films and Lubrication Approximation

In many applications the height of a fluid domain is small when compared to the horizontal extension. This is the case for example for wetting films or paint coats on a wall. In this case it is often possible to simplify the problem with free surface studied in the previous section considerably. 

Let H be a typical height of the film, L be a typical horizontal length scale and $\overline { { V } }$ a typical size of the vertical velocity components. In addition, we assume 

$$
\varepsilon := \frac {H}{L} \ll 1.
$$

We now denote the nondimensional variables with $\tt { a } ^ { \wedge }$ and obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = L (\widehat {x _ {1}}, \widehat {x _ {2}})  , \qquad \qquad x _ {3} = H \widehat {x _ {3}}  , \qquad t = (L / \overline {{V}}) \widehat {t}  , \\ (v _ {1}, v _ {2}) (t, x) = \overline {{V}} (\widehat {v _ {1}}, \widehat {v _ {2}}) (\widehat {t}, \widehat {x})  ,   v _ {3} (t, x) = \varepsilon \overline {{V}} \widehat {v _ {3}} (\widehat {t}, \widehat {x})  , \\ h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = H \widehat {h} (\widehat {t}, \widehat {x _ {1}}, \widehat {x _ {2}})  , \quad p (t, x) = \overline {{p}}   \widehat {p} (\widehat {t}, \widehat {x})  . \end{array}
$$

We will specify a typical value $\overline { { p } }$ for the pressure later. 

In the following we also denote differential operators with $\tt { a } ^ { \frown }$ if they correspond to the variables $\widehat { x }$ and $\widehat { t . }$ We hence denote 

$$
\partial_ {t} v _ {i} = \overline {{V}} \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \partial_ {\hat {t}} \widehat {v _ {i}}, \quad i = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {t} v _ {3} = \varepsilon \overline {{V}} \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \partial_ {\widehat {t}} \widehat {v} _ {3},
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {i}} v _ {j} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {v} _ {j}, \qquad i, j = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {3}} v _ {j} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \varepsilon^ {- 1} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {j}, \qquad j = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {i}} v _ {3} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \varepsilon \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {v _ {3}}, \qquad i = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {3}} v _ {3} = \varepsilon \overline {{V}} \frac {1}{H} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {3} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {3},
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {i} x _ {i}} v _ {j} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L ^ {2}} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}} \widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {v} _ {j}, \qquad i, j = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {3} x _ {3}} v _ {j} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L ^ {2}} \varepsilon^ {- 2} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3} \widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {j}, \qquad j = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {i} x _ {i}} v _ {3} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L ^ {2}} \varepsilon \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}} \widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {v} _ {3}, \qquad i = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {3} x _ {3}} v _ {3} = \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L ^ {2}} \varepsilon^ {- 1} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3} \widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {3},
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {i}} p = \frac {\overline {{p}}}{L} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {p}, \qquad i = 1, 2,
$$

$$
\partial_ {x _ {3}} p = \frac {\overline {{p}}}{L} \varepsilon^ {- 1} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {3}}} \widehat {p}.
$$

In addition, it holds that 

$$
\nabla h = \frac {H}{L} \widehat {\nabla} \widehat {h} = \varepsilon \widehat {\nabla} \widehat {h},
$$

$$
\nu = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla h | ^ {2}}} \binom{- \nabla h}{1} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) + \mathcal {O} (\varepsilon)  ,
$$

$$
\kappa = \nabla \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla h | ^ {2}}}\right) = \frac {1}{L} \varepsilon   \widehat {\varDelta}   \widehat {h} + \mathcal {O} \big (\varepsilon^ {2} \big)  .
$$

Let us neglect terms ofhigher order in $\varepsilon .$ Here $\overline { V }$ and $\overline { { p } }$ need to be scaled appropriately. In the Navier–Stokes equations the viscous part of the stress tensor and the pressure have to be scaled in the same way, i.e., 

$$
\mu \Delta v \approx \nabla p.
$$

From the first two components we can deduce that the scaling 

$$
\mu \frac {\overline {{V}}}{L ^ {2}} \varepsilon^ {- 2} = \frac {\overline {{p}}}{L}
$$

is meaningful, that is, 

$$
\overline {{V}} = \frac {\varepsilon^ {2} L}{\mu} \overline {{p}}.
$$

The tangential component of the force balance (7.83) on the upper boundary yields to leading order 

$$
\partial_ {\widehat {x _ {3}}} \widehat {v} _ {j} = 0 \text {   for   } j = 1, 2.
$$

In (7.83) the terms of lowest order have the factors $\gamma \varepsilon / L$ and ${ \overline { { p } } } .$ . Hence we choose 

$$
\overline {{p}} = \frac {\varepsilon \gamma}{L}.
$$

From the normal component of (7.83) it then follows that 

$$
\widehat {p} = - \widehat {\Delta} \widehat {h} + \mathcal {O} (\varepsilon) \text {for} \widehat {x _ {3}} = \widehat {h} (\widehat {t}, \widehat {x _ {1}}, \widehat {x _ {2}}).
$$

The Navier–Stokes equations yield after multiplication by $\frac { L ^ { 2 } \varepsilon ^ { 2 } } { \overline { { V } } \mu }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\varepsilon^ {2} \mathrm{Re} \big (\partial_ {\widehat {t}} \widehat {v} _ {1} + \widehat {v} _ {1} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {1}} \widehat {v} _ {1} + \widehat {v} _ {2} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {2}} \widehat {v} _ {1} + \widehat {v} _ {3} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {1} \big)} \\ & {\qquad = - \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {1}} \widehat {p} + \varepsilon^ {2} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {1} \widehat {x} _ {1}} \widehat {v} _ {1} + \varepsilon^ {2} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {2} \widehat {x} _ {2}} \widehat {v} _ {1} + \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3} \widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {1}} \end{array}
$$

with the Reynolds number $\mathrm { R e } = \varrho L \overline { { V } } / \mu$ . In addition, we get an analogous equation for $\widehat { v _ { 2 } }$ . For $\widehat { v _ { 3 } }$ it holds that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varepsilon^ {3} \mathrm{Re} \big (\partial_ {\widehat {t}} \widehat {v} _ {3} + \widehat {v} _ {1}   \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {1}} \widehat {v} _ {3} + \widehat {v} _ {2}   \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {2}} \widehat {v} _ {3} + \widehat {v} _ {3}   \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {3} \big) \\ = - \varepsilon^ {- 1} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {p} + \varepsilon^ {3} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {1} \widehat {x} _ {1}} \widehat {v} _ {3} + \varepsilon^ {3} \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {2} \widehat {x} _ {2}} \widehat {v} _ {3} + \varepsilon   \partial_ {\widehat {x} _ {3} \widehat {x} _ {3}} \widehat {v} _ {3}. \end{array}
$$

The equation $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol { v } = 0$ yields after multiplication by $L / { \overline { { V } } }$ 

$$
\widehat {\nabla} \cdot \widehat {v} = 0.
$$

Under the assumptions 

$$
\varepsilon^ {2} \mathrm{Re} \ll 1 \text { and } \varepsilon \ll 1
$$

we obtain as equations to leading order in the fluid region 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {3}} \widehat {x _ {3}}} \widehat {v _ {i}} = \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {i}}} \widehat {p} \text {for} i = 1, 2, \\ 0 = \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {3}}} \widehat {p}, \end{array}
$$

and on the free boundary $\widehat { x } _ { 3 } = \widehat { h } ( \widehat { t } , \widehat { x } _ { 1 } , \widehat { x } _ { 2 } )$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \partial_ {\widehat {x _ {3}}} \widehat {v} _ {i} = 0 \text {for} i = 1, 2, \\ \widehat {p} = - \widehat {\Delta} \widehat {h}, \\ \widehat {v} _ {3} = \partial_ {\widehat {t}} \widehat {h} + (\partial_ {\widehat {x _ {1}}} \widehat {h}) \widehat {v} _ {1} + (\partial_ {\widehat {x _ {2}}} \widehat {h}) \widehat {v} _ {2}, \end{array}\tag{7.89}
$$

where the last condition is just the kinematic boundary condition (7.81) which under the given scaling does not change its form. In the following we will drop the $\hat { . }$ . As $p$ does not depend on $x _ { 3 }$ we obtain 

$$
p (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}, x _ {3}) = - \Delta h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}).
$$

Integration of $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol { v } = 0$ with respect to $x _ { 3 }$ yields 

$$
0 = \int_ {0} ^ {h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2})} (\partial_ {x _ {1}} v _ {1} + \partial_ {x _ {2}} v _ {2}) d x _ {3} + v _ {3} (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}, h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2})) - v _ {3} (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}, 0).
$$

As $v _ { 3 } = 0$ for $x _ { 3 } = 0$ we deduce from the kinematic boundary condition (7.89) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \partial_ {t} h = - \int_ {0} ^ {h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2})} (\partial_ {x _ {1}} v _ {1} + \partial_ {x _ {2}} v _ {2}) d x _ {3} - (\partial_ {x _ {1}} h) v _ {1} - (\partial_ {x _ {2}} h) v _ {2} \\ = - \nabla \cdot \left(\int_ {0} ^ {h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2})} \binom {v _ {1}} {v _ {2}} d x _ {3}\right). \end{array}
$$

The equations $\partial _ { x _ { 3 } x _ { 3 } } v _ { i } = \partial _ { x _ { i } } p , i = 1 , 2$ , can be solved using $v _ { i } = 0$ for $x _ { 3 } = 0$ and $\partial _ { x _ { 3 } } v _ { i } = 0$ for $x _ { 3 } = h ( t , x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ as follows 

$$
v _ {i} (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}, x _ {3}) = \partial_ {x _ {i}} p (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) \left[ \frac {x _ {3} ^ {2}}{2} - h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) x _ {3} \right].
$$

We then obtain 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {h (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2})} v _ {i} d x _ {3} = \partial_ {x _ {i}} p (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) \left(- \frac {h ^ {3}}{3}\right).
$$

Altogether this leads to 

$$
\partial_ {t} h = \nabla \cdot \left(\frac {h ^ {3}}{3} \nabla p\right)
$$

or 

$$
\partial_ {t} h = - \nabla \cdot \left(\frac {h ^ {3}}{3} \nabla \Delta h\right).\tag{7.90}
$$

We have hence deduced from the free surface problem an equation which is formulated solely for the height. The Eq. (7.90) is called the thinfilm equation. Equations of the form 

$$
\partial_ {t} h = - \nabla \cdot (c h ^ {n} \nabla \Delta h) \text {with} c > 0, n > 0,
$$

allow for solutions with a compact support which is similar to the porous medium equation (cf. Exercise 7.25). Such solutions describe fluid films on a horizontal surface which do not wet the whole surface. The boundary of the support can as in the case of the porous medium equation be interpreted as afree boundary. 

## 7.12 Literature

Classical books on problems with free boundaries and variational inequalities are the books of Duvaut and Lions [30], Friedman [42], Kinderlehrer and Stampacchia [79], and Elliott and Ockendon [33]. A good reference for the analysis of convex optimization problems with side constraints is the book of Ekeland and Temam [32]. More information on the Stefan problem and on phase field equations can be found in the books of Brokate and Sprekels [15], Davis [26] and Visintin [136]. A nice introduction into the theory of phase transitions is given by Gurtin [60]. For information on the geometry of curves and surfaces we refer to books on differential geometry [9, 18, 35]. More information on free surfaces in fluid dynamics can be found in the book of Segel [118].

$$

for all $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } \big ( ( 0 , \infty ) \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \big )$ . Here $\nabla \varDelta h$ has to be defined piecewise. Show that there exists an $\alpha > 0$ such that $h ( t , \cdot ) \to \alpha \delta _ { 0 }$ as $t \searrow 0$ in the sense of distributions, i.e., for all $\zeta \in C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } (  { \mathbb { R } } ^ { d } )$ it holds that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} h (t, x) \zeta (x) d x \rightarrow \alpha \zeta (0) \text { as } t \searrow 0.
$$

Compute an $a > 0$ , such that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } h ( t , x ) d x = 1 } \end{array}$
