## Appendix A Function Spaces

We denote the vector space of all real-valued continuous functions on an open set $\mathcal { Q } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ with $C ^ { 0 } ( \varOmega )$ . Continuous functions with a domain of definition Ω and values in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } , \mathbb { C } \operatorname { o r } \mathbb { C } ^ { m }$ are denoted by $C ^ { 0 } ( \varOmega , \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , or by $C ^ { 0 } ( \varOmega , \mathbb { C } )$ , or $C ^ { 0 } ( \varOmega , \mathbb { C } ^ { n } )$ respectively, and we will use for the other function spaces which we will consider later a corresponding notation. For each number $k \in \mathbb N$ we define $C ^ { k } ( \varOmega )$ as the space of all k–times continuously differentiable functions on $\varOmega$ . The set of all arbitrarily often differentiable functions is denoted by $C ^ { \infty } ( \Omega )$ . For a function $\varphi : \Omega  \mathbb { R }$ we define its support to be 

$$
\operatorname{supp} \varphi := \overline {{\{x \in \Omega \mid \varphi (x) \neq 0 \}}}.
$$

The set $C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega )$ is the set ofall arbitrarily often differentiable functions whose support is a compact subset of $\varOmega$ 

In addition, we will use the function spaces 

$$
\begin{array}{l} C ^ {k} (\overline {{\Omega}}) := \left\{u: \overline {{\Omega}} \to \mathbb {R} \mid u \text {   is   continuous,   } u _ {| \Omega} \in C ^ {k} (\Omega) \right. \\ \quad \text { and   all   partial   derivatives   up   to } \\ \quad \text { the   order   } k \text {   can   be   continuously   extended   to   } \overline {{\Omega}} \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

If $\overline { { \varOmega } }$ is bounded one obtains that the spaces $C ^ { k } ( { \overline { { \varOmega } } } )$ are Banach spaces, i.e., they are complete normed vector spaces. A normed space is a vector space X with a mapping that maps each $x \in X$ to a real number $\| x \|$ such that 

(1) $\| x \| = 0$ if and only if $x = 0 .$ 

(2) $\| \alpha x \| = | \alpha | \| x \|$ for all scalars α and all $x \in X$ 

(3) $\| x + y \| \leq \| x \| + \| y \|$ for all x, $y \in X$ (triangle inequality). 

A sequence $( x _ { k } ) _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ in a normed space X converges if and only if an $x \in X$ exists such that the following holds: For al $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an $M \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
\left\| x _ {k} - x \right\| <   \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } k > M.
$$

A sequence $( x _ { k } ) _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ in a normed space X is a Cauchy sequence, if and only if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ an $M \in \mathbb { N }$ exists such that 

$$
\left\| x _ {k} - x _ {\ell} \right\| <   \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } k, \ell > M.
$$

A normed space X is complete and hence a Banach space if each Cauchy sequence in X has a limit $x \in X$ . If $\overline { { \varOmega } }$ is bounded it can be shown that $C ^ { k } ( { \overline { { \varOmega } } } )$ with the norm 

$$
\| u\|_{C^{k}(\overline{\Omega})}:= \max_{\substack{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}\\ |\alpha |\leq k}}\sup_{x\in \Omega}|\partial^{\alpha}u(x)|
$$

is a Banach space. Here $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { d } ) \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 } ^ { d }$ is a multi-index and $| \alpha | = \alpha _ { 1 } +$ $\cdots + \alpha _ { d }$ . We remark that $\| u \| _ { C ^ { 0 } ( \overline { { \varOmega } } ) }$ is the supremum of $| u |$ 

By $L _ { p } ( \Omega ) , 1 \le p \le \infty$ we denote the set of all real-valued measurable functions such that $| u | ^ { p }$ is Lebesgue–integrable. $L _ { p } ( \varOmega )$ with the norm 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\| u\|_{L_{p(\Omega)}}:= \biggl (\int_{\Omega}|u(x)|^{p}  dx\biggr)^{1 / p}\text{for} 1\leq p <   \infty ,\\ \| u\|_{L_{\infty (\Omega)}}:= \inf_{\substack{N\subset \Omega \\ N\text{null set}}}\sup_{x\in \Omega \setminus N}|u(x)|\text{for} p = \infty \end{array}
$$

is a Banach space. The condition (1) in the definition of the norm is fulfilled if we identify functions which differ on a set of measure zero with each other. We define equivalence classes as follows. We say that a function v is in the equivalence class u of the function u, i.e., $v \sim u$ , if 

$$
u = v \text {   almost   everywhere   in   } \Omega  .
$$

The set of all locally integrable functions is 

$$
L _ {1, \text { loc }} (\Omega) := \{u: \Omega \to \mathbb {R} \mid \text {   for   all   } D \subset \subset \Omega \text {   it   holds   } u _ {| D} \in L _ {1} (D) \}.
$$

Here $D \subset \joinrel \subset \varOmega$ means that D is bounded and ${ \overline { { D } } } \subset { \Omega }$ . For functions $u \in L _ { p } ( \varOmega )$ $v \in L _ { q } ( \varOmega )$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { p } + \frac { 1 } { q } = 1 } \end{array}$ Hölder’s inequality 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} | u (x) v (x) | d x \leq \left(\int_ {\Omega} | u (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \left(\int_ {\Omega} | v (x) | ^ {q} d x\right) ^ {1 / q}
$$

holds. For $p = q = 2$ this inequality is called the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. 

On the space $L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega )$ one can introduce the inner product 

$$
\langle u, v \rangle_ {L _ {2} (\Omega)} := \int_ {\Omega} u (x)   v (x)   d x  .
$$

An inner product on a real vector space H is a real-valued function $( x , y ) \mapsto \langle x , y \rangle$ such that 

(i) $\langle x , y \rangle = \langle y , x \rangle { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ a l l ~ } } x , y \in H ,$ 

(ii) $\langle \alpha x + \beta y , z \rangle = \alpha \langle x , z \rangle + \beta \langle y , z \rangle$ for all $\alpha , \beta \in \mathbb { R }$ and $x , y , z \in H$ 

(iii) $\langle x , x \rangle \geq 0$ for all $x \in X$ 

(iv) $\langle x , x \rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$ 

In a real vector space H with inner product the quantity 

$$
\| x \| = \sqrt {\langle x , x \rangle}
$$

defines a norm. If H is complete with respect to this norm we call H a Hilbert space. The space $L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega )$ with the above inner product is a Hilbert space. 

Often it makes sense to consider a weaker form ofthe classical notion ofderivative. If for an integrable function $u : \varOmega \to \mathbb { R }$ and a multi-index α an integrable function $v _ { \alpha } : \varOmega \to \mathbb { R }$ exists such that 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} u (x) \partial^ {\alpha} \varphi (x) d x = (- 1) ^ {| \alpha |} \int_ {\Omega} v _ {\alpha} (x) \varphi (x) d x
$$

for all $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega )$ , we call $\partial ^ { \alpha } u : = v _ { \alpha }$ the $\alpha ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ weak partial derivative of u. 

The Sobolev space $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ consists of all functions $u \in L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega )$ whose first partial derivative exists in a weak sense and for which these partial derivatives are square integrable. The space $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ with the inner product 

$$
\langle u, v \rangle_ {H ^ {1} (\Omega)} := \int_ {\Omega} (u (x) v (x) + \nabla u (x) \cdot \nabla v (x)) d x
$$

is a Hilbert space. 

Similarly one can define Sobolev spaces $H ^ { m } ( \Omega ) , m \geq 2$ by demanding that also higher weak partial derivatives are square integrable. 

In $L _ { 2 } ( \varOmega )$ and $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ functions belonging to an equivalent class differ on a set of measure zero. This means that it does not make sense to define boundary values as the boundary typically is a set of measure zero. However under suitable assumptions on the boundary $\partial \varOmega$ one can introduce boundary values for functions in $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ . A simple possibility to define zero boundary values is to consider the completion of $C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega )$ in $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} H _ {0} ^ {1} (\Omega) := \{u \in H ^ {1} (\Omega) \mid \text { there exists a sequence } (u _ {k}) _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \text { in } C _ {0} ^ {\infty} (\Omega), \\ \text { such that } \| u _ {k} - u \| _ {H ^ {1} (\Omega)} \to 0 \}. \end{array}
$$

One can interpret this space as the set of all functions in $H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ which have zero boundary values. The fact that functions in $H _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ have zero boundary values in a certain sense can also be justified more rigorously. 

If Ω is bounded one can show the Poincaré inequality for functions in $H _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ , i.e., there exists a constant $c _ { P } > 0$ which only depends on $\varOmega$ such that 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} | v | ^ {2} d x \leq c _ {P} \int_ {\Omega} | \nabla v | ^ {2} d x
$$

for all $v \in H _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ . If Ω is connected we also obtain such an inequality for functions $u \in H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ with $\textstyle \int _ { \Omega } u ( x ) d x = 0$ or for functions $u \in H ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ which are zero only on a part of ∂Ω having positive surface measure. 

Finally, we remark that for functions $u \in H ^ { m } ( \varOmega )$ in the case $m - { \begin{array} { l } { { \frac { d } { 2 } } } \end{array} } > 0$ a continuous function $v \in C ^ { 0 } ( \varOmega )$ ) exists such that $u \ : = \ : v$ holds almost everywhere in Ω. 

For further details and proofs of the stated results we refer to the books of Adams [2] and Alt [4]. 

# Appendix B Curvature of Hypersurfaces

The curvature of a curve in the plane is the change of direction per length. Let $I \subset \mathbb { R }$ be an interval and $y : I \to \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ be a differentiable curve which is parameterized by arc-length, i.e., $| y ^ { \prime } ( s ) | = 1$ for all $s \in I$ . Then $\tau : = y ^ { \prime } ( s )$ is a unit tangent of the curve and $y ^ { \prime \prime } ( s )$ measures the local change of the tangent per length. If $| y ^ { \prime \prime } ( s ) |$ is larger the tangent changes more quickly. The quantity $y ^ { \prime \prime } ( s )$ hence describes how much the curve is curved. 

For a curve $T \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ with unit normal we choose an arc-length parametrization $y$ such that $( \nu , y ^ { \prime } ( s ) )$ is positively oriented, i.e., det $( \nu , y ^ { \prime } ( s ) ) > 0$ . Differentiating $| y ^ { \prime } ( s ) | ^ { 2 } = 1$ leads to 

$$
0 = \frac {d}{d s} | y ^ {\prime} (s) | ^ {2} = 2 y ^ {\prime \prime} (s) \cdot y ^ {\prime} (s).
$$

This implies that $y ^ { \prime \prime } ( s )$ is a multiple of $\nu$ and we define 

$$
\kappa = y ^ {\prime \prime} (s) \cdot \nu
$$

as the curvature ofthe curve $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } }$ . Choosing instead of ν the normal $- \nu$ we change the sign of the curvature $\kappa .$ 

We now consider a smooth surface $\varGamma$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ with unit normal $\nu .$ . In this case we can define a normal curvature for each tangential direction $\tau$ . This normal curvature is defined as the curvature of the plane curve which is obtained by intersecting the plane spanned by $\nu$ and $\tau$ with the surface $\varGamma$ . Now let $\kappa _ { 1 }$ and $\kappa _ { 2 }$ be the minimal and maximal values of the normal curvature. The values $\kappa _ { 1 }$ and $\kappa _ { 2 }$ are called the principal curvatures and the mean curvature is defined as 

$$
\kappa = \kappa_ {1} + \kappa_ {2}.\tag{B.1}
$$

Strictly speaking $\frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \kappa _ { 1 } + \kappa _ { 2 } )$ is the mean curvature. However, nowadays most mathematicians use (B.1) as the definition of mean curvature as this leads to simpler expressions in most cases. 

We now want to define curvature generally for hypersurfaces $\boldsymbol { \Upsilon }$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , i.e., for smooth $( d - 1 )$ –dimensional surfaces of $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . In order to do so we first of all consider tangential derivatives of functions which are defined on $\boldsymbol { { \cal { r } } }$ . For $x \in { \boldsymbol { T } }$ we define by $T _ { x } T$ the space of all tangential vectors at a point $x \in \Upsilon$ . Let $f : Y \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m } , m \in \mathbb { N }$ be a smooth function, $x \in { \boldsymbol { T } }$ and $\tau \in T _ { x } \mathcal { T }$ . Let us choose a curve $y : ( - \varepsilon , \varepsilon )  Y$ with $y ( 0 ) = x$ and $y ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \tau$ and define 

$$
\partial_ {\tau} f (x) = \frac {d}{d s} f (y (s)) \big | _ {s = 0}.
$$

One can show that this definition does not depend on the specific choice of the curve $y$ as long as $y ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \tau$ holds. In addition, it follows that the mapping $\tau \mapsto \partial _ { \tau } f$ is linear with respect to $\tau _ { \ast }$ , i.e., for $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , \tau \in T _ { x } \boldsymbol { \mathcal { T } }$ with $\tau = \alpha _ { 1 } \tau _ { 1 } + \alpha _ { 2 } \tau _ { 2 }$ it holds that 

$$
\partial_ {\tau} f (x) = \alpha_ {1} \partial_ {\tau_ {1}} f (x) + \alpha_ {2} \partial_ {\tau_ {2}} f (x).
$$

We can now consider tangential derivatives of the normal vector ν. The mapping 

$$
\begin{array}{c} W _ {x}: T _ {x} \Upsilon \to T _ {x} \Upsilon  , \\ \tau \mapsto - \partial_ {\tau} \nu \end{array}
$$

is called Weingarten map of $\boldsymbol { \Upsilon }$ in the point x. As $\partial _ { \tau }$ is linear with respect to $\tau$ we obtain that the Weingarten map $W _ { x }$ is linear. The identity 

$$
(\partial_ {\tau} \nu) \cdot \nu = \partial_ {\tau} \frac {1}{2} | \nu | ^ {2} = \partial_ {\tau} \frac {1}{2} = 0
$$

implies that $\partial _ { \tau } \nu$ lies in the tangent space $T _ { x } T$ . This implies that $- \partial _ { \tau } \nu$ is a mapping from the tangent space $T _ { x } T$ into itself. For two smooth vector fields $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } : Y  \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ with $\tau _ { 1 } ( x ) , \tau _ { 2 } ( x ) \in T _ { x } \mathcal { T }$ for all x it follows with the help of $\tau _ { 2 } \cdot \nu = 0$ 

$$
(\partial_ {\tau_ {1}} \tau_ {2}) \cdot \nu = (\partial_ {\tau_ {1}} \tau_ {2}) \cdot \nu - \partial_ {\tau_ {1}} (\tau_ {2} \cdot \nu) = - \tau_ {2} \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {1}} \nu .\tag{B.2}
$$

We now consider a local parametrization $F : D  Y$ . The symmetry of the second derivative of $F$ implies the symmetry of the Weingarten map with respect to the Euclidean inner product in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ which we will demonstrate in what follows. The vectors 

$$
t _ {1} = \partial_ {1} F, \ldots , t _ {d - 1} = \partial_ {d - 1} F
$$

form a basis of the tangent space. For arbitrary tangential vectors we find a representation 

$$
\tau_ {1} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \alpha_ {i} \partial_ {i} F, \quad \tau_ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \beta_ {i} \partial_ {i} F
$$

and we compute with the help of $\nu \cdot \partial _ { i } F = 0 , \partial _ { t _ { i } } F = \partial _ { i } F { \mathrm { f o r } } i = 1 , \dots , d - 1$ and the linearity of the tangential derivative 

$$
\begin{array}{c} W _ {x} (\tau_ {1}) \cdot \tau_ {2} = - \left(\partial_ {\tau_ {1}} \nu\right) \cdot \tau_ {2} = \nu \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {1}} \tau_ {2} = \nu \cdot \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} \alpha_ {i} \beta_ {j}   \partial_ {t _ {i}} \left(\partial_ {j} F\right) \\ = \nu \cdot \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} \alpha_ {i} \beta_ {j}   \partial_ {i} \partial_ {j} F = \nu \cdot \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} \alpha_ {i} \beta_ {j}   \partial_ {j} \partial_ {i} F \\ = \nu \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {2}} \tau_ {1} = - \tau_ {1} \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {2}} \nu = \tau_ {1} \cdot W _ {x} (\tau_ {2}). \end{array}
$$

As the Weingarten map is symmetric real eigenvalues $\kappa _ { 1 } \leq \dots \leq \kappa _ { d - 1 }$ exist with corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors $v _ { 1 } , \dotsc , v _ { d - 1 } \in T _ { x } \mathcal { Y }$ . It holds that 

$$
\kappa_ {i} = \kappa_ {i} | v _ {i} | ^ {2} = - (\partial_ {v _ {i}} \nu) \cdot v _ {i} = (\partial_ {v _ {i}} v _ {i}) \cdot \nu .
$$

This implies that $\kappa _ { i }$ is the normal curvature in the direction $v _ { i }$ . The quantities $\kappa _ { 1 } , \ldots , \kappa _ { d - 1 }$ are called principal curvatures. The curvatures $\kappa _ { 1 }$ and $\kappa _ { d - 1 }$ , respectively, minimize and maximize the following quadratic form which corresponds to the Weingarten map 

$$
(\tau , \tau) \mapsto (- \partial_ {\tau} \nu) \cdot \tau = (\partial_ {\tau} \tau) \cdot \nu
$$

under all $\tau \in T _ { x } \boldsymbol { \mathcal { T } }$ with $| \tau | = 1$ , see Exercise 7.7. The bilinear form $( \tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } ) \mapsto$ $( - \partial _ { \tau _ { 1 } } \nu ) \cdot \tau _ { 2 }$ is called the secondfundamentalform of $\boldsymbol { r }$ . One obtains that 

$$
\kappa = \operatorname{trace} W _ {x} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \kappa_ {i}
$$

and for $d = 3$ this is just the definition (B.1). In the following, the quantity is called mean curvature of $\boldsymbol { r }$ at $x .$ . 

For an orthonormal basis $\left\{ \tau _ { 1 } , \dots , \tau _ { d - 1 } \right\}$ of the tangent space $T _ { x } T$ we can compute the mean curvature as follows 

$$
\kappa = \operatorname{trace} W _ {x} = - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \left(\partial_ {\tau_ {i}} \nu\right) \cdot \tau_ {i} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \left(\partial_ {\tau_ {i}} \tau_ {i}\right) \cdot \nu .
$$

Defining the tangential divergence $\nabla _ { T }$ · of a vector field $f$ on $\boldsymbol { r }$ by 

$$
\nabla_ {\gamma} \cdot f = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} \tau_ {i} \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {i}} f
$$

one obtains the compact form 

$$
\kappa = - \nabla_ {\gamma} \cdot \boldsymbol {\nu}.
$$

Hence, the mean curvature is just the negative tangential divergence of the normal. 

Often the mean curvature has to be computed in a situation in which a natural but not orthonormal basis $\{ t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { d - 1 } \}$ of the tangent space is present. We will shortly discuss the linear algebra needed in this case. As a special case we will compute the mean curvature of a graph. Let $\left\{ \tau _ { 1 } , \dots , \tau _ { d - 1 } \right\}$ be an orthonormal basis of the tangent space. Then there exists a matrix $A = ( a _ { i j } ) _ { i , j = 1 } ^ { d - 1 }$ such that 

$$
\tau_ {k} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {d - 1} a _ {k i} t _ {i}.
$$

As $\{ \tau _ { 1 } , . . . , \tau _ { d - 1 } \}$ is orthonormal it follows 

$$
\delta_ {k \ell} = \tau_ {k} \cdot \tau_ {\ell} = \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} a _ {k i} a _ {\ell j} t _ {i} \cdot t _ {j} = (A G A ^ {\top}) _ {k \ell}
$$

with 

$$
G = (g _ {i j}) _ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} := (t _ {i} \cdot t _ {j}) _ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1}.
$$

It hence holds that $A G A ^ { \top } = \operatorname { I d }$ and hence 

$$
G = A ^ {- 1} (A ^ {- 1}) ^ {\top}, \quad G ^ {- 1} =: (g ^ {i j}) _ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} = A ^ {\top} A.
$$

For a vector field $f : Y \to \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ we now obtain from the fact that $\partial _ { \tau } f$ is linear with respect to $\tau .$ , 

$$
\nabla_ {\gamma} \cdot f = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {d - 1} \tau_ {k} \cdot \partial_ {\tau_ {k}} f = \sum_ {i, j, k = 1} ^ {d - 1} a _ {k i} a _ {k j} t _ {j} \cdot \partial_ {t _ {i}} f = \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} g ^ {i j} t _ {j} \cdot \partial_ {t _ {i}} f.
$$

We now assume that $\boldsymbol { { \cal { r } } }$ is given as a graph 

$$
\Upsilon = \left\{x = (x ^ {\prime}, x _ {d}) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} \mid x _ {d} = h (x ^ {\prime}), x ^ {\prime} \in D \right\},
$$

where 

$$
h: D \to \mathbb {R}, \quad D \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {d - 1} \text { open },
$$

is twice continuously differentiable. A basis of the tangent space is given as 

$$
t _ {1} = (e _ {1}, \partial_ {1} h), \ldots , t _ {d - 1} = (e _ {d - 1}, \partial_ {d - 1} h),
$$

where $e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { d - 1 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d - 1 }$ are the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb { R } ^ { d - 1 }$ . In this case we have $g _ { i j } = \delta _ { i j } + \partial _ { i } h \partial _ { j } h$ and a simple computation yields 

$$
g ^ {i j} = \delta_ {i j} - \frac {\partial_ {i} h \partial_ {j} h}{1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}.
$$

As unit normal we obtain 

$$
\nu = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} (- \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h, 1) ^ {\top}.
$$

For a quantity $f : Y  \mathbb { R }$ with $f ( x ) = f ( x ^ { \prime } , h ( x ^ { \prime } ) ) = \widehat { f } ( x ^ { \prime } )$ one obtains $\partial _ { t _ { i } } f =$ $\partial _ { i } \widehat { f }$ and we compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \kappa = - \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} g ^ {i j} t _ {j} \cdot \partial_ {t _ {i}} \nu = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} g ^ {i j} t _ {j} \cdot \partial_ {i} (\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h, - 1) ^ {\top} \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} g ^ {i j} \partial_ {i j} h \\ = \frac {\Delta_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}} - \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {d - 1} \frac {\partial_ {i} h}{(1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}) ^ {3 / 2}} \partial_ {j} h   \partial_ {i j} h \\ = \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} \cdot \left(\frac {\nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h}{\sqrt {1 + | \nabla_ {x ^ {\prime}} h | ^ {2}}}\right). \end{array}
$$
